lead: Batch adsorption is a fixed amount of solid stirred with a fixed volume of liquid until equilibrium. A fixed bed is a column packed with adsorbent through which fluid flows continuously. The bed cleans the fluid well until the adsorption zone reaches the exit. The breakthrough curve records that arrival. Industry uses batch tests to rank adsorbents and fixed beds to polish water, recover solvents and clean air. The curve tells the operator when to stop feeding and switch or regenerate the bed.
prereq: You need: 6.1 and 6.2 for adsorbent capacity and isotherms, and Unit 2, Mass Transfer Coefficients and Interphase Transfer, for the idea of a mass-transfer zone.

blocks.text: In a batch test, W grams of dry adsorbent are added to V litres of solution at initial concentration C0. The mixture is shaken until the liquid concentration stops changing at Ce. Solute lost from the liquid equals solute gained by the solid. No reaction and no volume change are assumed. The loading q is the mass of solute held per mass of dry adsorbent.

blocks.where: q is the loading (mg/g); C0 and Ce are initial and equilibrium liquid concentrations (mg/L); V is solution volume (L); W is dry adsorbent mass (g); if W is given in kg, convert to g before dividing.

blocks.text: A high q at low Ce means a good adsorbent. The pair (Ce, q) must also sit on the isotherm from 6.2. Batch tests are quick, but they give equilibrium capacity, not how fast a column works.

Feed with solute concentration C0 enters the top of a packed column. Clean adsorbent starts at the bottom. Three regions form. Near the inlet, the adsorbent is saturated and in equilibrium with C0; this is the saturated zone. Ahead of it is the mass-transfer zone (MTZ), a moving band where concentration falls from C0 to nearly zero. Below the MTZ the adsorbent is still fresh. The MTZ moves down much slower than the fluid.

At first the exit concentration C is almost zero. When the front of the MTZ reaches the exit, C rises. The plot of C/C0 against time is the breakthrough curve. By custom, breakthrough is often C/C0 = 0.05 and exhaustion is C/C0 = 0.95. The exact limits are a design choice; state them when you use them.

An early breakthrough means a long unused bed (much of the capacity is still fresh) or poor kinetics. Confirm with LUB ≈ H(1 − q_b/q_e): a small q_b gives a large LUB. A sharp curve means a narrow MTZ and good use of capacity. A long tail means slow intraparticle diffusion, axial dispersion or channeling, or an unfavourable (near-linear) isotherm; a favourable isotherm sharpens the front. Some syllabi cover stagewise and moving-bed adsorbers as separate contactors; only the fixed bed is treated here. Ion-exchange columns use the same curve; see 6.4.

sections.h3: Capacity from the curve and unused bed

blocks.text: For constant feed flow Q, solute fed up to time t is C0Qt. Solute leaving is Q∫C dt. Solute held by the bed is the difference. The exact loading on the bed at time t is the area between C0 and the breakthrough curve.
q(t) = (Q/W) ∫ (C0 - C) dt, from 0 to t
blocks.where: q(t) is bed loading at time t (mg/g); Q is feed flow (L/min); W is dry adsorbent mass (g); C0 is feed concentration (mg/L); C is exit concentration at time t (mg/L).

blocks.text: If C is near zero up to breakthrough tb, then q_b ≈ C0Qtb/W. This is the breakthrough capacity, not the full capacity. The shortcut q_e ≈ C0Qte/W with exhaustion time te is an upper estimate because solute leaves after breakthrough. The exact q_e integrates the whole curve.
f_unused = (q_e - q_b) / q_e    and    LUB ≈ H(1 - q_b/q_e)
blocks.where: f_unused is the fraction of bed capacity unused at breakthrough; q_b and q_e are loadings at breakthrough and exhaustion (mg/g); LUB is length of unused bed; H is bed depth (m).

blocks.text: A short LUB means the bed is well used at breakthrough. A long LUB means part of the column is still fresh when the exit begins to rise. Some syllabi cover stagewise and moving-bed adsorbers as separate contactors; only the fixed bed is treated here, and fixed-bed design depends on the breakthrough curve.

figure.caption: Exit concentration C/C0 against time. Breakthrough is at 30 min (C/C0 = 0.05); exhaustion is at 90 min (C/C0 = 0.95). The S-shape is the mass-transfer zone passing the exit.

spec.title: Breakthrough curve
spec.aria: An S-shaped breakthrough curve rising slowly to C/C0 about 0.05 at 30 min, then steeply to 0.95 at 90 min.

examples.question: A column contains W = 1.5 kg adsorbent. Feed concentration C0 = 80 mg/L and flow Q = 2 L/min. Breakthrough (C/C0 = 0.05) is at tb = 30 min; exhaustion (C/C0 = 0.95) is at te = 90 min. Take exit concentration as negligible up to breakthrough, and use the zero-exit shortcut for the exhaustion capacity. Find q at breakthrough in mg/g and the fraction of bed capacity unused at breakthrough if capacity at exhaustion is used.
steps: Convert adsorbent mass: W = 1.5 kg = 1500 g.
Solute fed up to breakthrough: C0Qtb = 80 mg/L × 2 L/min × 30 min = 4800 mg.
Breakthrough loading: q_b = 4800 mg / 1500 g = 3.2 mg/g.
Solute fed up to exhaustion by the shortcut: C0Qte = 80 × 2 × 90 = 14400 mg.
Exhaustion loading estimate: q_e = 14400 mg / 1500 g = 9.6 mg/g.
Note: 0.667 equals 1 − tb/te. Since the shortcut overestimates q_e, the true unused fraction is somewhat below 66.7%; the exact value needs the integral of C0 − C.
examples.answer: q_b = 3.2 mg/g; q_e = 9.6 mg/g; unused fraction ≈ 0.667, about 66.7%. This is an upper estimate: the shortcut overestimates q_e, so the true unused fraction is somewhat below 66.7%.
examples.check:
q_b = 80 * 2 * 30 / 1500
q_exh = 80 * 2 * 90 / 1500
unused = (q_exh - q_b) / q_exh
print(q_b)
print(q_exh)
print(round(unused, 3))

traps: Using exhaustion time te in q_b: breakthrough capacity uses tb, not te.
Treating C/C0 = 0.05 as exactly zero without saying so; the shortcut is an approximation.
Reporting q in mg/g when concentrations are mg/L and W is in kg without converting kg to g.
Confusing the breakthrough curve (C/C0 against time) with the isotherm (q against C).
Calling q_e from C0Qte/W exact after breakthrough; after breakthrough solute leaves, so exact q_e needs the integral of C0 - C.

quiz.q: Define breakthrough in a fixed-bed adsorber.
quiz.a: Breakthrough is the time when exit concentration reaches a chosen fraction of feed concentration, often C/C0 = 0.05.

quiz.q: Why does a breakthrough curve have an S shape?
quiz.a: The mass-transfer zone has a finite width. As it passes the exit, C rises from near zero to near C0 over the time the zone takes to leave; diffusion and equilibrium spread the front.

quiz.q: A bed has W = 2.0 kg, C0 = 50 mg/L, Q = 3 L/min, tb = 40 min. Estimate q_b assuming C is near zero before breakthrough.
For the same bed, te = 120 min and q_e = 9.0 mg/g. Find the unused fraction at breakthrough using q_b = 3.0 mg/g.
A column shows early breakthrough and a long tail. Suggest two causes.
quiz.a: Early breakthrough can come from channeling, too short a bed or poor kinetics. A long tail can come from slow intraparticle diffusion, axial dispersion/channeling, or an unfavourable (near-linear) isotherm.

quiz.q: Why is q_b from C0Qtb/W not the full equilibrium capacity? How would you improve the estimate?
quiz.a: It assumes C = 0 before tb, so it ignores the bed capacity still unused at breakthrough and any solute that leaks early. To improve q_b, integrate Q(C0 − C) up to tb using measured C values and divide by W; to get the full capacity, integrate to te.

quiz.q: State the usual C/C0 values for breakthrough and exhaustion.
quiz.a: Often C/C0 = 0.05 for breakthrough and C/C0 = 0.95 for exhaustion; these are conventions, not fixed laws.

beyond: Not for the exam. Fixed-bed adsorption is the basis of pressure-swing and temperature-swing adsorption for air separation, natural-gas drying and solvent recovery. Water treatment uses granular activated carbon columns with the same breakthrough logic. Chromatography is a fixed bed run in pulses, so its peaks are breakthrough curves in time. Research replaces the sharp front with numerical solutions of coupled diffusion and isotherm equations. Search for adsorption breakthrough curve, length of unused bed and mass transfer zone.
